title: Lamentations 3:1–18
context: Lamentations 3 is the book’s central and longest poem. In the Hebrew it is an acrostic of twenty-two three-line stanzas: the lines of each stanza begin with the same letter, and the stanzas move through the alphabet, giving 66 verses (chapters 1, 2, and 4 are also acrostics, and chapter 5 keeps the twenty-two-line count without the alphabetic pattern). Many readers suggest the form gives ordered shape to overwhelming grief, though the poet does not state a purpose. Where the narrator and Zion speak in chapters 1–2, chapter 3 opens with a single voice, the afflicted man: “I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of his wrath” (3:1). His identity is debated. Some, following the common tradition that links the book with Jeremiah (the book itself is anonymous), hear the prophet, whose sufferings in Jeremiah 20 and 37–38 offer echoes; others hear a representative sufferer whose story models the way through judgment for the whole people; others hear personified Zion or the nation speaking as one man, since the voice later shifts to “we” (3:40–47). These readings run across both traditions, and elements of them are often combined. In 3:1–18 the man describes the LORD’s hand against him in images of darkness, siege, chains, a walled road, a bear and a lion, an archer’s target, bitterness, and gravel, ending with his hope nearly gone (3:18). The LORD is not named until 3:18; the repeated “he” is the LORD, whose wrath the book elsewhere connects with Jerusalem’s sin (1:5, 1:8, 1:18). Both traditions read this section as honest lament that Scripture itself gives the afflicted to pray, and both hold that the wrath described is just judgment rather than cruelty, while refusing to rush the sufferer past his pain.

verses.text: I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of his wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: The afflicted man opens with “I am the man,” speaking as one who has seen affliction under “the rod of his wrath.” Arminian readers stress that the wrath is the LORD’s just response to his people’s sin (compare 1:5, 1:18), real and personal, and that the man’s honest testimony is meant to be heard by all who share the city’s ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the rod as the LORD’s real chastening, ordered by his hand rather than by chance (compare Isaiah 10:5, where Assyria is the rod of his anger). Shared ground: both hear a single voice carrying the community’s grief, whether that voice is Jeremiah, a representative sufferer, or Zion personified, and both treat the wrath as just.

verses.text: He has led me and caused me to walk in darkness, and not in light.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has led me and caused me to walk in darkness, and not in light.” Arminian readers note that the language of leading, usually the shepherd’s care (compare Psalm 23:2–3), is turned upside down, and they hear the bitter experience of a people who walked away from the light and now feel God’s leading as judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s hand directing even the darkness, so that judgment is never outside his governance, and they hear the lament as permitted, faithful speech rather than rebellion. Shared ground: both traditions take darkness here as the felt absence of God’s favor, and both let the sufferer say so without correcting him.

verses.text: Surely he turns his hand against me again and again all day long.
verses.arminianNotes: The man feels the LORD’s hand turned against him “again and again all day long,” the same hand that once delivered Israel (compare Deuteronomy 26:8). Arminian readers emphasize the relational weight of this reversal: covenant unfaithfulness has real consequences, and God responds to his people as they have responded to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the repetition underlines God’s active, purposeful judgment rather than random misfortune, and they place even unrelenting affliction within his wise and righteous rule. Shared ground: both hear the felt relentlessness of suffering as part of honest lament, not as a statement that God has stopped being God to his people.

verses.text: He has made my flesh and my skin old. He has broken my bones.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has made my flesh and my skin old. He has broken my bones.” Arminian readers note the bodily toll of grief and judgment, akin to the psalmist’s broken bones in confession (compare Psalm 32:3; 51:8), and they see room for restoration as the sufferer turns to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who wounds in order to heal (compare Hosea 6:1), and they treat the language as poetic description of total affliction, body and soul, under his hand. Shared ground: both traditions recognize that suffering touches the whole person and that Scripture does not ask the afflicted to minimize bodily pain.

verses.text: He has built against me, and surrounded me with bitterness and hardship.
verses.arminianNotes: The man describes himself as a besieged city, built against and surrounded “with bitterness and hardship,” an image that fits Jerusalem’s siege. Arminian readers see the personal and national story intertwined: the man’s experience mirrors the city’s, and the siege is the outcome of a long-refused call to return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the siege imagery as the LORD’s ordained judgment working through Babylon’s armies, while Babylon remains responsible for its own cruelty. Shared ground: both traditions hear the poem binding one sufferer to the whole city’s ruin, and both treat the bitterness as real rather than merely symbolic.

verses.text: He has made me dwell in dark places, as those who have been long dead.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has made me dwell in dark places, as those who have been long dead” (compare Psalm 143:3, a close echo). Arminian readers hear the near-death despair of the faithful in crisis and note that the complaint is still spoken in God’s hearing, which keeps the relationship open even in darkness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the likeness to the grave as the deepest form of the LORD’s chastening, from which only he can raise his people (compare Psalm 88:6). Shared ground: both traditions accept that believers may feel as good as dead, and both refuse to treat that feeling as proof that God has abandoned them.

verses.text: He has walled me about, so that I can’t go out. He has made my chain heavy.
verses.arminianNotes: The man is walled in and chained, unable to go out (compare Job 19:8, where Job says God has walled up his way). Arminian readers emphasize the felt loss of freedom and see it as a consequence of sin, while noting that the poem moves toward hope rather than leaving the captive without recourse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wall and the chain as images of God’s sovereign restraint in judgment, the same hand the man later confesses has redeemed his life (3:58). Shared ground: both traditions hear the captivity language as fitting the exile, and both read it as lament rather than a final verdict on the sufferer.

verses.text: Yes, when I cry, and call for help, he shuts out my prayer.
verses.arminianNotes: “When I cry, and call for help, he shuts out my prayer.” Arminian readers treat this as the honest experience of unanswered prayer under judgment (compare 3:44), and they note that the man keeps praying, which shows that he has not given up on God even when God seems closed to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the felt silence of God as part of the chastening and note that it is later answered when the LORD draws near (3:55–57). Shared ground: both traditions affirm that believers may experience prayer as shut out, and that the experience is to be brought to God rather than hidden from him.

verses.text: He has walled up my ways with cut stone. He has made my paths crooked.
verses.arminianNotes: His ways are walled up with cut stone and his paths made crooked, the image of the blocked road (compare Hosea 2:6; Job 19:8). Arminian readers see God blocking a path that led away from him, a severe mercy meant to turn the wanderer back, though the poem here voices only the pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereign hand ordering even the crooked paths of his people, so that no turn of their lives escapes his purposes. Shared ground: both traditions hear the complaint as the experience of being unable to see a way forward, and both treat it honestly before the hope of 3:21.

verses.text: He is to me as a bear lying in wait, as a lion in hiding.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD is “as a bear lying in wait, as a lion in hiding,” startling language that Hosea 13:7–8 also uses for God’s judgment. Arminian readers hear the shock of covenant love turned to threat when it has been spurned, and they keep the image within the poem’s lament rather than making it a full portrait of God’s character.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as the terror of God’s just wrath, which faith must confess honestly rather than soften, while trusting the mercy the poem will soon recall (3:22–23). Shared ground: both traditions read the predator images as metaphor within lament, and both hold that wrath is not the whole word about God.

verses.text: He has turned away my path, and pulled me in pieces. He has made me desolate.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has turned away my path, and pulled me in pieces. He has made me desolate.” Arminian readers follow the predator image and see desolation as the fruit of judgment on a people who refused to return, while the word desolate also echoes the ruined city and Zion’s own cry (compare 1:4, 1:13).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the man torn apart by God’s hand as a picture of the depth of the chastening, from which only the same hand can restore him (compare Hosea 6:1). Shared ground: both traditions take the desolation seriously as both personal and corporate, and neither treats it as the end of God’s dealings with his people.

verses.text: He has bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD bends his bow and sets the man “as a mark for the arrow” (compare 2:4; Job 16:12). Arminian readers hear the sense of being singled out, and they note that the lament gives words to those who feel targeted by God without requiring them to explain their suffering before they may speak of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the archer image as the LORD’s deliberate, purposeful judgment and emphasize that nothing in it is accidental, even when the sufferer cannot see its purpose. Shared ground: both traditions let the image stand as lament and do not use it to claim that every sufferer is being punished for a specific sin.

verses.text: He has caused the shafts of his quiver to enter into my kidneys.
verses.arminianNotes: The arrows reach the man’s “kidneys,” the inmost self in Hebrew idiom. Arminian readers see the wound reaching the depths of his emotional and spiritual life, and they note that such honest language belongs to faith, since it is spoken within a prayer that will soon turn toward hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inner wounding as the sharpest edge of God’s chastening, reaching beyond outward loss to the heart, and they read it as discipline within the covenant rather than rejection. Shared ground: both traditions recognize that God’s dealings touch the inner life and that grief at that depth is not a failure of faith.

verses.text: I have become a derision to all my people, and their song all day long.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have become a derision to all my people, and their song all day long” (compare 3:63; Jeremiah 20:7). Arminian readers note the added pain of mockery from one’s own people and see in it the isolation of the faithful sufferer, a theme many readers in both traditions also trace forward to Christ (compare Psalm 69:11–12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scorn as part of the burden the representative sufferer bears, and many read it christologically without denying its original setting in Jerusalem’s ruin. Shared ground: both traditions hear the real pain of social shame in suffering and refuse to treat ridicule of the afflicted as a light thing.

verses.text: He has filled me with bitterness. He has stuffed me with wormwood.
verses.arminianNotes: Bitterness and wormwood fill the man (compare Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15, where the LORD threatens wormwood as judgment). Arminian readers see the fulfillment of prophetic warnings the people had refused, and they note that the image returns in the man’s own plea that his affliction be remembered (3:19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wormwood as the bitter cup of judgment God himself serves, a just sentence rather than a malicious one, and they connect it with the hope that the same God remains the man’s portion (3:24). Shared ground: both traditions read the bitterness as real covenant judgment and as language the afflicted may honestly use.

verses.text: He has also broken my teeth with gravel. He has covered me with ashes.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has also broken my teeth with gravel. He has covered me with ashes.” Arminian readers hear images of humiliation and mourning, perhaps bread mixed with grit and the ashes of grief (compare Psalm 102:9), and they see the man brought low as the city itself has been brought low.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the humbling as the LORD’s work, pressing the sufferer into the dust before lifting him (compare 3:29), and they hold that even this abasement serves God’s purposes for his people. Shared ground: both traditions treat the images as poetic expressions of utter humiliation, not as literal details to be pressed.

verses.text: You have removed my soul far away from peace. I forgot prosperity.
verses.arminianNotes: For the first time the man addresses God directly: “You have removed my soul far away from peace. I forgot prosperity.” Arminian readers note the turn from speaking about God to speaking to him, and they see in it the persistence of relationship even when peace and well-being are only a memory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss of peace as the sharpest point of the chastening, and they note that the direct address shows faith still clinging to the God who wounds. Shared ground: both traditions hear the move to the second person as significant, and both affirm that a sufferer may tell God that peace feels lost.

verses.text: I said, “My strength has perished, along with my expectation from the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: The man confesses that his strength and his “expectation from the LORD” have perished, naming the LORD for the first time in the poem. Arminian readers stress the honesty of near-despair and note that the very next lines begin the turn toward hope, so the poem itself does not condemn the one who feels hope is gone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this as the low point from which God’s faithfulness will lift the man, and they emphasize that hope is restored not by his own strength but by remembering the LORD’s mercies (3:21–23). Shared ground: both traditions treat the confession pastorally, as a cry the LORD hears rather than a final verdict.
